newsitem.title: USA: U.S. hog prices seen rising on slow herd expansion.
newsitem.headline: U.S. hog prices seen rising on slow herd expansion.

text.p: A slower than expected expansion of the U.S. hog herd reported by the U.S. Agriculture Department on Thursday should result in higher cash and futures prices in the second half of the year, livestock analysts said.
"The industry is, at this stage, hard pressed to expand aggressively," said Chuck Levitt, senior livestock analyst for Alaron Trading Corp.
However, price action in pork futures and cash markets may take their cue from developments in Taiwan, where pork exports were banned last week because of a disease outbreak.

The USDA reported all hogs on farms as of March 1 at 99 percent of last year, hogs kept for breeding at 101 percent, and hogs kept for market at 99 percent. All three categories were in line with the average estimates, but the winter pig crop and farrowing intentions, which reflect hog producers' plans to breed, were less than expected.

The December/February pig crop was 100 percent of last year, at the low end of expectations, and March/May and June/August farrowing intentions were 100 and 102 percent, both below the low end of expectations.
"If we had any expansion going on in this country right now it would have showed up in that March/May farrowings intentions figure," Levitt said.
Analysts attributed the slower than expected expansion of the U.S. hog herd to pork producers' difficulties in coping with environmental and regulatory issues.

Panelists on a Chicago Mercantile Exchange market roundtable said emphasis on odor-related problems has kept expansion down in traditional hog producing states while new hog operations have sprung up in non-traditional hog producing areas of the West and Southwest.

"(Odor) is the biggest issue people have and the thing they all use to stop the placement of hog facilities themselves. Environmental regulations are a real problem," said CME panelist Dale Durchholz, marketing analyst for AgriVisor Services Inc.
Panelist Ron Plain, livestock marketing economist at University of Missouri, said, "There has been a real shift and the rapid growth right now does seem to be coming from the southern High Plains."
This is the same area the cattle industry moved to 30 years ago, Plain added. Lower population densities in the area have reduced the impact of odors from livestock operations.
Analysts agreed that hog prices overall will rise going into the second half of the year.

Hogs on a live basis in the second quarter could average $54 to $57 per cwt, third quarter $53 to $56 and fourth quarter $50 to $53. On a lean value basis, third quater estimates ranged from $84 to $86 and last quarter $76 to $78 per cwt, analysts said.

Price projections for futures were harder to come by, as analysts were uncertain of the continuing impact of Taiwan's pork export ban. But all analysts surveyed look for August futures to gain about one cent per pound and possibly more on Monday.

"Based on the report, I can't (see) more hogs than a year ago until December, and every deferred contract that we have on the board is anywhere from $4 to $10 under year-ago prices.... I remain very optimistic for the second and third quarter of this year," said panelist and CME floor trader Michael Downs, of Downs Research Group.

Levitt noted that slow expansion and expected lighter hog slaughter rates in the second half of the year are especially bullish to the pork industry as the Japanese "gate price" safeguard comes off July 1, and by the second half of this year Japan will be running out of pork stocks following the Taiwan export ban.

"Our export demand for pork by the third quarter should be expanding very rapidly and we are not going to have a significant increase in pork production to meet that increased export demand," Levitt said.
